newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Separatist Georgian region votes for president.
newsitem.headline: Separatist Georgian region votes for president.

text.p: Georgia's separatist region of South Ossetia voted on Sunday in a presidential election which the Georgian government says is a setback to peace moves after a bloody conflict.
The 32,000 registered voters in the sparsely-populated region, which declared independence from Georgia in 1990 and was at war from 1991 to 1992, faced a choice of four candidates.

Current leader Lyudvig Chibirov, a 64-year-old ethnographer who is formally Chairman of Parliament, was expected to face a stiff challenge for the newly-created post from "prime minister" Vladislav Gabarayev.

Chibirov, candidate of the South Ossetian Communist Party which dominates the rugged mountainous region's political life, has ruled since 1993 and engineered moves to find a peaceful settlement with the Georgian government.

He was also instrumental in efforts to create the post of President because he said it was needed to end political infighting. "Right now the concentration of power in a single person's hands is needed," he told Reuters.
He said he was ready at any time to continue negotiations with Tbilisi over South Ossetia's status.
Although he says he favours talks, Gabarayev takes a tougher line with Georgia.

He has told voters that if elected he will guarantee that South Ossetia will secede from Georgia and be allowed to join Russia. Many Ossetians want to unite with their ethnic kin across the border in Russia's republic of North Ossetia.
But South Ossetia's entreaties to Moscow to be taken under its wing have been ignored in the past, except among ultra-nationalist politicians like Vladimir Zhirinovsky.

South Ossetia, a chunk of territory about the size of Luxembourg, declared independence as the Soviet Union was disintegrating and Georgia was gripped by a wave of nationalism which minority groups feared.
Clashes between ethnic Ossetians, an ancient Caucasus ethnic group whose members speak a language related to Farsi, and local Georgians turned into war in 1991.

Late Georgian nationalist President Zviad Gamsakhurdia sent in armed forces in an unsuccessful attempt to crush the independence drive. Fighting with Ossetian volunteers killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands more homeless.
Most Georgians have fled the region but several thousand still live in scattered villages where the election is not being held.
Although Chibirov still pays lip service to independence, economic woes, crime and the realisation that no country is about to recognise South Ossetia have led him to seek compromises with Tbilisi.
This culminated in the signing of a preliminary political accord earlier this year.
Chibirov dismissed criticism from both Georgia and Russia, which have said the vote could derail the peace process.
"The decision to have a presidential system had nothing to do with external politics. It is only a matter of domestic politics. I don't understand the reaction of our neighbours," he said.
By midday (0700 GMT) some 31 percent of voters in the regional capital, Tskhinvali, had cast their ballots.
The South Ossetian Central Elections Commission expected a turnout of 80 percent across the region by the time polls closed. Results are expected on Monday.
